title: Christology
summary: These passages contribute several portraits to biblical reflection on Jesus. Second Samuel 7 promises David an enduring dynasty and speaks of the king as God’s son. Psalm 2 presents a royal figure whose rule reaches the nations. Isaiah 11 pictures a ruler from Jesse’s line marked by justice and the Spirit; Isaiah 53 portrays a suffering servant who bears the people’s infirmities and wrongdoing, without naming him in the cited passage. Luke 24 depicts the risen Jesus interpreting Moses and the Prophets in relation to himself. In Acts 2, Peter proclaims Jesus as Lord and Messiah and reads Davidic Scripture in light of the resurrection. The royal and servant images are connected in Christian interpretation, but they should not be collapsed into one literary role.
historical_context: The references move from Israel’s royal and prophetic writings to New Testament interpretation. Second Samuel 7 presents a promise concerning David’s house and royal succession; Psalm 2 is a royal poem about God’s king. Isaiah 11 looks toward a ruler from Jesse’s line, while Isaiah 53 describes a servant’s suffering and its effects for others. Luke 24 and Acts 2 are post-resurrection scenes in which Jesus and Peter interpret Israel’s Scriptures. These texts show how the New Testament witnesses represented here read Israel’s royal and prophetic traditions; they are not a single historical account or a full history of messianic expectation.
canonical_context: The cluster begins with the promise to David’s house, adds the royal language of Psalm 2, and places beside it Isaiah’s images of a just ruler and a suffering servant. Luke 24 presents Jesus interpreting Moses and the Prophets after the resurrection; Acts 2 has Peter use Davidic Scripture to proclaim Jesus as Lord and Messiah. These connections show how early Christian texts interpret Jesus through Israel’s Scriptures. They do not make every royal or servant passage interchangeable, or establish that each originally referred to Jesus in the same way.
literary_context: The passages use different forms: a dynastic promise in Second Samuel 7, a royal psalm in Psalm 2, prophetic portraits in Isaiah 11 and 53, a post-resurrection interpretation scene in Luke 24, and a public speech in Acts 2. Acts 2 makes its scriptural reasoning visible as Peter cites Davidic texts; Luke 24 presents Jesus interpreting the larger witness of Moses and the Prophets. Isaiah 53’s servant is not named in the cited passage, so the text’s original referent should not be assumed from its later Christian use alone.
covenantal_significance: Second Samuel 7 links Israel’s royal hope with God’s promise to David’s house. Psalm 2 and Isaiah 11 imagine rule under God’s authority, while Isaiah 53 portrays suffering and the bearing of others’ wrongdoing. Luke 24 and Acts 2 show New Testament writers interpreting Jesus through Israel’s Scriptures, including Davidic promise and resurrection. Together the passages hold authority, justice, suffering, and vindication in view. Their connection matters for Christian readings of Jesus, while their distinct literary settings and claims remain visible.
canonical_role: Christology serves as a theological anchor, connecting doctrinal concepts, canonical development, and related passages across Scripture.

interpretive_notes.note: Read Christology in its immediate context before generalizing.
Do not flatten distinct passages into one slogan; let the canon keep its own shape.

common_questions: How does Christology fit the biblical storyline?
What should readers avoid when interpreting Christology?
